nameStory: The 'crane's-bill' name comes from the plant's distinctive seed pods, which have a long, pointed beak that looks remarkably like a crane's bill. When the seeds are ripe, this 'bill' splits open dramatically, flinging seeds away from the parent plant. The 'meadow' part tells us where this European native likes to grow - in open grasslands and meadows.
description: Meadow crane's-bill is a robust perennial wildflower that forms impressive clumps up to 3 feet across. This hardy plant produces hairy stems topped with delicate, saucer-shaped flowers in pale violet or lavender. Originally from the mountains of Europe and Asia, it's built to survive harsh winters and creates a lovely mounded display in gardens and naturalized areas. The deeply divided leaves give it a lacy, elegant appearance even when not in bloom.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Five-petaled saucer-shaped blooms in pale violet or lavender, about an inch across, with delicate dark veining visible on the petals when you look closely

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided palmate leaves that feel rough and hairy to the touch, cut into 5-7 narrow segments that radiate from a central point like fingers on a hand

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading clumps that can reach 3 feet across, with multiple hairy stems rising from the base, giving it a full, mounded appearance

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The signature crane's-bill seed pods are unmistakable - long, pointed beaks that split dramatically when ripe, making a slight popping sound as they fling seeds

habitat: In New England, meadow crane's-bill is typically found in cultivated gardens, around old homesites, and occasionally naturalized in meadows and field edges. It prefers well-drained soils in full sun to partial shade and can tolerate a range of soil conditions. Look for it near old farmsteads or in perennial gardens where it may have escaped cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with fresh green, deeply-cut leaves forming attractive mounds. Flower buds begin developing on hairy stems in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with showy pale violet flowers opening in succession. The distinctive hairy stems and saucer-shaped blooms are most visible now.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen and the characteristic crane's-bill pods split open dramatically. Leaves may turn reddish before dying back to the ground.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to ground level, with only the root system surviving underground until spring growth returns.

funFact: When meadow crane's-bill seed pods ripen, they don't just split open - they actually explode with enough force to launch seeds up to 15 feet away, making a tiny popping sound you can hear if you're close enough during seed dispersal time!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with wild geranium, but meadow crane's-bill has paler violet flowers (not the deeper pink-purple of wild geranium) and much more deeply divided, narrower leaf segments. Remember: meadow = paler flowers and more finely cut leaves.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these true geraniums with the common garden 'geraniums' sold at nurseries - those are actually pelargoniums from South Africa! True geraniums like meadow crane's-bill are hardy perennials, while garden 'geraniums' are tender and need to be brought indoors for winter in New England.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives. Its pale violet flowers distinguish it from the deeper pink wild geranium, and its large size and broad clumping habit separate it from smaller species like Herb Robert or the various weedy crane's-bills.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
